source_text: Loquitur ergo ad Valerium: Attende quibus se existimat adversum nos huic praemisso titulo consonare; Deus - inquit - qui Adam ex limo fuerat fabricatus, Evam construxit e costa, et dixit: " Haec vocabitur Vita, quoniam mater est omnium viventium " [n4] . Non quidem ita scriptum est, sed quid ad nos? Solet memoria falli in verbis, dum tamen sententia teneatur. Nec Evae nomen ut appellaretur Vita, Deus imposuit, sed maritus. Sic enim loquitur: " Et vocavit Adam nomen uxoris suae "Vita", quoniam mater est omnium viventium " [n5] . Stupenda doctoris eruditio, qui ne paululum quidem a Scripturarum sinit sermone deflecti. Imperitiam nostram arguit; sed oblivioni veniam dare dignatur, qua factum erat ut ego dicerem nomine Vitae a Deo mulierem nuncupatam; ita per occasionem brevem, et eruditus apparere studuit, et benignus. Sed ut non est admiranda diligentia, nominatorem feminae comperisse; ita impudentia non ferenda est, velle ignoscere quod culpare non possis. Non enim ita in meo opere legitur, sicut in commentis huius tenetur. Ego quippe posito legis testimonio, quod dixisse rerum Creator ostenditur: " Non est bonum solum esse hominem; faciamus ei adiutorium simile sui " [n6] . Quid est hoc - inquio - " Non est bonum esse solum hominem "? Numquid Deus aliquid fecerat, quod non bonum iure dici posset; maxime qui omnia non solum bona, sed etiam bona valde fecerat? Quomodo ergo ait: " Non est bonum solum esse hominem "? quo sermone non reprehenditur creaturae status, sed ostenditur humano generi perniciosam unionem esse potuisse, nisi ministerio diversi sexus successio germinasset. Nam si etiam Adam speretur potuisse immortalis fieri, nisi deliquisset; tamen manifestum est, patrem eum numquam fieri potuisse, nisi reperisset uxorem, quae de latere dormientis assumpta, prima compellatione cui operi parata esset audivit: " Haec vocabitur Vita, quoniam mater est omnium viventium ". Quo sermone monstratum est, neminem deinceps hominum vel esse posse, vel vivere, qui non conceptus beneficio substitisset [n7] . Cum ergo clareat, in re quidem non magni ponderis, tamen nihil a me ita fuisse prolatum, ut illud praeter impudentiam singularem quisquam possit arguere; inusta est nota publicae falsitatis egentissimo omnium, qui cum vult donare quod non tenet, uno tempore pariter delinquit, et penuria iuris, et ambitu largitatis.
pass_a_gloss: He speaks therefore to Valerius: Attend by what arguments he thinks he agrees, against us, with this heading set forth beforehand; God — he says — who had fashioned Adam from mud, built Eve from a rib, and said: 'She will be called Life, because she is the mother of all the living.' It is not indeed so written, but what is that to us? Memory is accustomed to be deceived in words, provided nevertheless the sentence is held. Nor did God impose the name on Eve that she should be called Life, but the husband. For thus he speaks: 'And Adam called the name of his wife Life, because she is the mother of all the living.' Astonishing learning of the teacher, who does not allow even a little to be deflected from the speech of the Scriptures. He accuses our ignorance; but he deigns to give pardon to forgetfulness, by which it had been done that I said the woman was named by God with the name Life; thus through a short occasion he studied to appear both learned and kind. But as the diligence is not to be admired, to have found out the namer of the woman, so the shamelessness is not to be borne, to want to forgive what you cannot blame. For it is not so read in my work as it is held in this man's inventions. I, indeed, the testimony of the law having been set down, which the Creator of things is shown to have said: 'It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself.' What is this — I say — 'It is not good for the human being to be alone'? Had God made something that could rightly be called not good, especially he who had made all things not only good but even very good? How therefore does he say: 'It is not good for the human being to be alone'? By which speech the status of the creature is not blamed, but it is shown that solitude could have been ruinous for the human race unless a succession had sprouted by the ministry of the other sex. For if even Adam is hoped to have been able to become immortal had he not sinned, nevertheless it is manifest that he could never have become a father unless he had found a wife, who, taken from the side of the sleeper, heard at the first addressing for what work she had been prepared: 'She will be called Life, because she is the mother of all the living.' By which speech it was shown that thereafter no one of humans could either exist or live who had not been substituted by the benefit of conception. Since therefore it is clear that, in a matter indeed not of great weight, nevertheless nothing was so brought forth by me that anyone could accuse it besides singular shamelessness, the mark of public falsehood has been branded on the most destitute of all, who when he wants to give what he does not hold, at one time equally offends, both by poverty of right and by the canvassing of generosity.

pass_b_english: He therefore says to Valerius: “Notice the arguments by which he thinks he agrees, against us, with the heading set out above. He says, ‘God, who had fashioned Adam from mud, built Eve from a rib and said: She will be called Life, because she is the mother of all the living’ (Genesis 3:20). That is not actually how it is written, but what does that matter to us? Memory commonly goes wrong over words, provided the meaning is retained. Nor was it God who named Eve Life, but her husband. The text says: ‘And Adam called his wife’s name Life, because she is the mother of all the living’” (Genesis 1:31) (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.12).

What astonishing learning in this teacher, who allows not even the slightest departure from Scripture’s language! He rebukes my ignorance, yet deigns to pardon the lapse of memory through which I had supposedly said that God called the woman by the name Life. He thus used a small opportunity to try to appear both learned and kind. But just as identifying who named the woman is no remarkable feat of diligence, so his shamelessness is intolerable when he wants to forgive something he cannot blame. For my work does not read as his inventions have it. I first quoted the Law’s testimony, where the Creator of all things is shown saying, “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself” (Genesis 2:18). Then I said: “What does this mean, ‘It is not good for the human being to be alone’? Had God made anything that could rightly be called not good, especially when he had made everything not merely good but very good (compare Genesis 1:31)? How, then, does he say, ‘It is not good for the human being to be alone’? These words do not criticize the creature’s condition; they show that being alone could have been ruinous for the human race unless a succession of descendants had sprung up through the service of the other sex. For even if Adam may be thought capable of becoming immortal had he not sinned, it is nevertheless clear that he could never have become a father unless he had found a wife. Taken from his side while he slept, she heard at her first naming the work for which she had been prepared: ‘She will be called Life, because she is the mother of all the living.’ This statement showed that thereafter no human being could either exist or live without coming into existence through the benefit of conception” (compare Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.12).

It is therefore clear that, although the matter is not very weighty, I said nothing that anyone could criticize without extraordinary shamelessness. The stamp of public falsehood has been branded on this most destitute of men. By trying to give away what he does not possess, he offends in two ways at once: he lacks the right to do it, and he courts applause for his generosity.
